en: Regarding the *Fahua jing shu*, from the perspective of the principle that the Ultimate Teaching is also fully present, it can be summarized as follows: the person [of the Buddha] is the True and Responsive [Bodies], while the teaching is the Expedient and Real.
This scripture elucidates this completely; thus, one knows that the principle is profound and cannot be fully exhausted by words. This is the long [passage].
The first section clarifies that the merit of this sutra is explained as being inexhaustible.
The subsequent verses describe the merit of those who propagate it; this is not a mere elaborate discourse.
This is the general purport of the passage.
This clearly explains the merit of the person who transmits the sūtra;
it does not exhaustively clarify the reason for the sūtra’s circulation. It merely indicates that one who upholds the sūtra is endowed with complete virtue.
This is stated according to the sūtras. To speak in brief:
it is intended to clarify that the virtues of the Tathāgata are indeed immeasurable.
It is called "essential" because it clarifies four meanings.
These four refer to that which belongs to all Tathāgatas.
This phrase intends to clarify the raising of the hand and the lowering of the head.
All are the foremost principle.
This is the first [section] clarifying the reality of his teaching.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing sovereign spiritual powers:
This is the second clarification of the skillful means regarding form:
manifesting the long through the short must necessarily seek correspondence with the Way;
thus, manifesting the short within the long reveals the injury to the ultimate truth and the sovereign power of spiritual efficacy.
The treasury of all the Tathāgata’s secret essentials is this third vehicle of skillful means; for the sake of sentient beings,
the Tathāgata does not differentiate between boundaries nor seek after any single one [of them].
Regarding all the profoundly deep matters of the Tathāgata:
although the ultimate Dharmakāya manifests birth and extinction through expedient means for the sake of sentient beings, its true body is so profound that it is devoid of transition or change.
This is the fourth true jewel of the body.
This sutra fully elucidates all speech;
it is appropriate that everything be revealed and explained within this sutra.
From this point onward, the fourth section concludes by exhorting the two individuals.
Because the principles of this scripture are profound and its benefit to sentient beings is vast,
you must not fail to expound it in the future.
At that time, for this reason, it is said that after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one should single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra].
The phrase "exhorting their disciples" refers to encouraging those under one's guidance; the subsequent passage exhorts the teacher himself.
From the passage "In whatever land" onwards,
the text formally raises the profound principle and exhorts [the reader] to practice;
it refers to the place where one recites the sutra and the location where one dwells.
"In all these places, one should erect stupas and make offerings, for the sake of honoring the profound sutras.
Why is this so? [The passage] beginning with 'Why is this so?
explains the reason why it is not the case that the Way was attained at the place of birth."
Regarding the construction of stupas at the places where the Wheel of Dharma was turned and where [the Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa:
if one constructs such a stupa for the sake of propagating the One Vehicle and making offerings to the Lotus Sutra, even if it is known by external consciousness, [it is meritorious].
Riding upon principle and focusing the mind, whether birth or cessation arises, the myriad practices are fulfilled.
At the place where the Way is attained, one upholds the essential purport of the sutra;
that is the place where the Wheel of Dharma is turned. Knowing that the Sage should pass on, that is the place of Nirvana.
The explanations within these verses do not eulogize the objects of the chapter.
First, regarding the request for circulation by the bodhisattvas, there are three initial verses.
Second, [they eulogize] the five kinds of auspicious omens mentioned above.
Among these, only the tongue-mark emitting light, the clearing of the throat, and the snapping of fingers shaking the earth are praised in verse.
The fifth point, the ten directions’ respectful admiration, is omitted from the verse.
As for the body emitting countless rays of light:
To clarify that the capacities of sentient beings vary in ten thousand ways and their responses are likewise not uniform,
there follow eleven and a half verses beginning from "Having extinguished the conditions for devotion.
This concludes the third section above, which cites the principles of the sutra to exhort the second reliance on the profound Dharma.
The first three verses precisely eulogize the fact that the merit of those who uphold this sutra is exceedingly great,
beginning from the passage "those who can uphold this sutra" and so forth.
To extensively praise his immeasurable merits and exhort him to propagate the sutra is to see me;
it is to clarify that the ultimate truth of the Buddha is used as the essence, and to realize that this principle resides within the mind—this is what is meant by "seeing."
Furthermore, because the Buddha conforms to [the capacity of] beings yet never departs from the holy, he is seen constantly. If one can, in this final age,
master the sutras and transform sentient beings, one will not only see the Buddha,
but even the absence of compliance constitutes the offering of Dharma.
From the section beginning with "Regarding the meaning of all phenomena" onwards, the first four [sections] clarify one's own practice (*svacaryā*).

From this point forward, it clarifies external transformation (*paravivartana*); the mastery of principles and resources for benefiting others is called "unimpeded," whereby one can guide and benefit sentient beings according to their faculties.
It is said that he "walks in the world" because he extinguishes evil and gives rise to good.
To be able to extinguish the darkness of sentient beings is precisely to extinguish evil.

From the passage on "teaching and transforming" onwards, it clarifies the complete arising of goodness. Since the benefit of the sūtra extends to both humans and devas, one must not fail to be diligent regarding the future; thus, [the teaching] should be made accessible for future generations.
From this point onward, one verse and a half conclude the fourth section, which summarizes and exhorts the two individuals.
From here below, within the text of the "Entrustment" chapter (*Parīndanā-parivarta*),
it concerns future generations.
This is the second passage.
It records that the Tathāgata personally spoke these words of entrustment.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata has entrusted this Great Dharma to the bodhisattvas.
To propagate and disseminate [the teachings] in an evil age is a matter of heavy karmic burden for a bodhisattva.
Second, they desire that the two supports remain in the future.
To propagate and disseminate this sutra so that it shall not be interrupted for successive generations,
it is therefore called the "Chapter on Entrustment."
Within this chapter, there are four textual sections in total.
The first begins from the very beginning and concludes with the phrase "universally heard and known."

The first section, from the beginning up to "so that they may attain the stage of non-retrogression," intends to clarify how the Tathāgata personally and earnestly exhorts and instructs the two types of reliance. The second section, from "For what reason?
onwards until "the grace of all Buddhas," intends to clarify how the Tathāgata encourages those two types of reliance.
At the time of its circulation,
it should correspond to those two bases;
at the time of universal transformation, it should accord with them.
The *Buddha-compiled Verse* (Fó chéng sòng): Section Three, from "At that time, the various Bodhisattvas...

down to "...may you have no concerns," clarifies that the various Bodhisattvas respectfully accept and shall carry out the instructions. Section Four, from "When the command was given, Śākyamuni... down to the end of the prose section.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata has finished preaching this sutra. He then utters the proclamation for dispersal according to one's will (*yathāsukha-vissajjana*).
As for "stroking the crowns of the heads of the immeasurable bodhisattvas with his right hand":
To clarify that this extends from one hand to the crowns of many heads is also a display of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
It is called "concealing the supernatural power while manifesting it through verbal proclamation," meaning:
"I have cultivated and accumulated this rare, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) over immeasurable [aeons]."
To clarify that when the Tathāgata was on the stage of causal practice,
he cultivated causes over vast eons before finally attaining the Dharma-body as his fruit;
therefore, it is said to be "difficult to obtain."
Because the Tathāgata wishes to cause all beings to realize this Great Dharma together with him, he entrusts it to the two supports.
To ensure that the transmission and transformation continue to be heard so that it does not fall into ruin for a thousand years, he says, "You."
You should single-mindedly propagate this Dharma,
causing it to increase and flourish extensively,
so that all sentient beings may everywhere hear and know it.
From the section beginning with "Why is this so?
onwards, the second part of this chapter exhorts those two bases;
the Buddha has composed verses for this purpose.
Therefore, so that you may be able to circulate [this teaching] in future ages, you must certainly study the four dharmas of the Buddha.
First, understand that the Tathāgata possesses great compassion.
Second, it clarifies that the Tathāgata is free from all stinginess and parsimony.
Third, it clarifies that because the Tathāgata bestows the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings, he is said to be fearless.
Fourth, it clarifies that the Tathāgata is the great donor to all sentient beings.
If one can practice the four dharmas of the Tathāgata,
one will be able to circulate this sutra in the evil age; therefore,
it is said that one should also study the Tathāgata’s dharma accordingly and not give rise to stinginess.
From the passage beginning with "In future ages, if there are men or women... onwards, he exhorts them regarding the characteristics of the two reliances (*dvaya-niśraya*):
that for those of great faculties (*mahā-indriya*), the Dharma should be bestowed according to their capacity.
This is because it speaks of only one [aspect].
It says, "One who has faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom should be expounded this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*," beginning from the passage, "If there are sentient beings... and so forth.
Because he teaches the three vehicles to those of inferior faculties and roots,
it is said that "within other profound dharmas, he instructs, benefits, and gladdens them."
The Master of the Sūtras, seeking out the text of this sūtra, extensively expounded the Lotus Sūtra;
he must have known this beforehand through his presence in the void,
for such a thing has never occurred since time immemorial.
Within this context, it is known through the testimony of the initial statement that [the Buddha] "arose from the Dharma" and "conferred the empowerment by touching the crown of the head.
From here below, up until the end of the scripture in the passage concerning future generations, is the third major section: the teaching on the two reliances.
In future ages, the application of the Dharma shall circulate.
However, how could these two Great Beings merely rely on the literal text of the holy teachings?
In their desire to propagate [the Dharma], they intended to address these two bases.
During the period when those first learning the vehicle are in the midst of practicing asceticism, one should cause the teachings to circulate;
one should enter universally through skillful means like Bhaiṣajyarāja, and like Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara,
one should preach mantras to provide protection.
Just as one relies on a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for dhāraṇīs, you,
Wondrously Adorned and Reverent, act as a spiritual friend, just like Pure Treasury and the others.
The two individuals who were exhorted and inspired are like Samantabhadra;
because this serves as a point of proof, the citation is placed here.
If one were to discuss the proper sequence, it should instead be situated after the section on Aśoka (Fujaku).
Within this chapter, there are generally two sections. First, from the beginning down to "all were filled with joy," the purpose is to clarify the past ascetic practices of Bhaiṣajyarāja;
thus, Puṣpadanta requests the Buddha to speak of them. Second, from "The Buddha said" onwards until the end, it clarifies the offerings.

The Section on the Propagation of the Medicine King’s Ascetic Practices for the Future Period. Third: From "At that time, that Buddha, as all sentient beings... onwards, until "...his merit is the greatest."
This clarifies that the Medicine King Bodhisattva, in both the present and the future, burns his own body to dispel suffering and propagate the Dharma;
such is the guidance provided.
At that time, the Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of all sentient beings.
To clarify that within the Dharma of Adornment through Vision, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* circulates and provides benefit through its principles,
he immediately attained the Samādhi of the Physical Body and felt the profound weight of the Buddha’s grace.
Furthermore, because his robes were worn through by exposure to moisture,
and because he exhausted his wealth and life-force to provide for offerings,
these ascetic practices manifest the profound principles of the Way.

Because he had attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he said: "I should now make offerings to the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; it is not as good as making offerings with my own body.

This passage is intended to clarify that among sentient beings, there are many who have attained the Way through the practice of burning the body and sacrificing their lives, as recorded in the scriptures.
It is said that this is not as good as making offerings with one's own body.
This is intended to clarify that giving up the body is also a form of giving up wealth.
Why, then, do you say that the "True Dharma Offering" is superior?
However, their realizations of the Way differ.
Desiring to attain liberation by burning the body, they sacrifice themselves for the sake of penetrating the Great Dharma;
thus, it is said that this constitutes a true offering of the Dharma.
It is like the case of the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha), where one attains understanding of the Mahāyāna by means of smelling fragrances.
Regarding the first type of giving, the bestowal of material wealth to nourish the physical body is considered inferior;
that which leads to the penetration of the Hīnayāna through such wealth is considered middling.
Today, because one penetrates the Mahāyāna Dharma through wealth, it is considered supreme.

Therefore, it is said that when the body reaches its end at the one thousand two hundredth year, all sentient beings will be extinguished; the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) shall then shift, and this burning and warding off—burning the desires and subduing them again—is accomplished.
One should know that there are differences among great beings according to their faculties, which may be hidden or manifest;

it is not intended to point specifically to the abundance of merit, but rather to say that though burning one's finger is difficult—wounding the tendons and the bone—to be able to do so constitutes a great achievement.
If one can uphold this sutra, the merit thereof exceeds even that;

for with a mind superior to inferior forms, one clarifies the profound principles of the sutra and exhorts others to circulate it. Fourth, from "For example, like all rivers and streams" (*yathā sarva-nadī-pravāhāḥ*) down to "this sutra can save all sentient beings," [the text explains the merit].

This section clearly elucidates that the principles of this sutra are profound and its benefits for sentient beings far-reaching; it also points out that this sutra surpasses other scriptures in many respects. Second, based on the future, it explains that it should be widely circulated. Fifth, from the passage beginning with "From this sutra, one can save all sentient beings" down to "the merit obtained is likewise immeasurable," [the text concludes].
The preceding section clarifies that the principle is profound.

How is it known that the following section clarifies how this sutra can eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings and benefit immeasurable numbers, thereby attesting to its profound principle? The sixth [section] begins from: "If there be anyone who, having heard this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja'... and so forth.
One should thus maintain such a mind.
I entrust this chapter and exhort these two individuals to receive,
uphold, and circulate it during the final age.
If there are women who, upon hearing this chapter, are able to receive and uphold it,
they should first exhort their disciples that in the future they ought to listen and receive it with diligent effort.
This applies from the period following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata for up to fifty years.
He exhorts that Dharma Master to circulate those objects.
From the passage beginning with "from the outset" onwards, it clarifies the extinction of evil;
thus it says, "one is no longer afflicted by greed and desire."
From "Having obtained the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers" onwards, it clarifies the arising of wholesome qualities.
From "At that time, all Buddhas" onwards, it extensively elucidates how the Buddhas praise the profound and far-reaching virtues of those who uphold this sutra.
From this point, beginning with "O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña," [the Buddha] formally exhorts the Dharma Master that he should, in the future, propagate this sutra and benefit sentient beings.
From the passage beginning with "O Nakṣatrarāja, if you see anyone who receives and upholds this sutra... and so forth.

From the passage beginning with "Exhorting those disciples that in the future they should make offerings to Dharma-preachers who seek the Great Dharma" and continuing with "those who have already sought the Buddha-way," the text concludes by exhorting them to make offerings.
Seventh, from the point where the "Chapter on the Medicine King" (Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta) is preached onwards.
This clarifies the benefits for that time.
Regarding the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound," this person is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body who previously manifested in the eastern direction.
As there was a karmic affinity for him here in this land, he was summoned by the emission of light.
Within this chapter, there are five sections in total. The first, from the beginning down to "and preached the Dharma for them," clarifies the sphere of practice of that Sublime Sound.
Regarding this, the emission of light follows the brief exposition and precedes the detailed exposition;
it is the first [of the two].

The reason for emitting these two lights is as follows: the emission of the "flesh-knot" light signifies that the fundamental knot is supreme, manifesting the highest excellence and loftiness of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The emission [of light] from between the eyebrows signifies the principle of the Middle Way, which is free from partiality. Second, from the passage beginning with "Having already explained... down to "...because they also wish to hear this Lotus Sutra," [the meaning is as follows].

Clarifying the signs of the future appearance of Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound). Third, from Mañjuśrī’s address to the Buddha, "What roots of goodness has this bodhisattva planted? down to "Thus he benefits immeasurable sentient beings."

The fourth section, from "When this 'Chapter on the Exquisite Sound' was being spoken, Gadgadasvara arrived together with [the Buddha]" onwards, concludes with the "Samādhi of the Physical Body. This extensively elucidates the virtuous conduct of the Exquisite Sound.
Clarifying the Benefits of Coming and Going. From the fifth section, "The Chapter on Coming and Going," onwards, the benefits to be realized are clarified.
Within this second stage, [the practitioner] has long required the foundation of various virtues, up to the path and the great samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All of these are the sūtra author’s praises of Gadgadasvara’s virtues;
they are not the Tathāgata’s own exposition of his conduct and qualities.
If [the virtues] had already been clarified within this section, [there would be no need for further praise].
Furthermore, why is it necessary to list his virtuous conduct again?
From the passage beginning with "From the Buddha Amitābha down to the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom" onwards,
it is intended to clarify that Gadgadasvara, being about to set out, respectfully requested permission from that Buddha to come here.
From the point where the Buddha has finished instructing Gadgadasvara onwards, the Tathāgata Pure Flower (Vimalakusuma) addresses Gadgadasvara with the intent of focusing on the precepts.
As for why he first exhorts the various junior bodhisattvas: it is because...
That minor bodhisattva did not realize that Śākyamuni was manifesting a superior transformation body in a sixteen-foot form, and thus he conceived a sense of arrogance and disrespect.
For this reason, [the Buddha] cautioned him, saying: "Go, but do not give rise to thoughts of inferiority."
From the passage where the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara addresses his own Buddha downward,
it is intended to clarify that Gadgadasvara receives empowerment through looking up to [the Buddha's] grace;
furthermore, as he intends to go to the Sahā world, Gadgadasvara is a practitioner of the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmamegha-bhūmi*).

How could it be that they must wait for the Buddha’s empowerment before being able to come? Since the text speaks of "minor practices" and "contemplation" as being provisional, it says that "all are the Tathāgata’s [empowerment].
This refers to the section beginning from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara did not rise... and so forth.
This clearly explains the signs preceding the arrival of Gadgadasvara.
By first observing these auspicious omens,
this great assembly is enabled to know in advance that the Great Being Gadgadasvara, whose nature is the Dharma-body, is approaching.

To show that those who have come from afar to hear the Lotus Sūtra have manifested a profound and mysterious principle, thereby inspiring in them diligent reverence and providing mutual benefit, [the text] begins from the passage:
"At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, having seen these lotus flowers, addressed the Buddha... and so forth.
This clarifies that when this great assembly beheld these auspicious signs, they did not understand their cause and thus gave rise to doubts;
from the passage beginning with "The Buddha having spoken" onwards,
it clarifies that Gadgadasvara will come to resolve those sentences of doubt.

He said, "I have come here desiring to make offerings and to hear the Lotus Sūtra, precisely for the sake of propagating this sūtra. From the passage where Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, "What roots of goodness does this bodhisattva possess? and so forth.
The third section clarifies his virtuous conduct.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, Mañjuśrī poses three questions; second, the Tathāgata answers those questions.
"What roots of goodness did they plant, and what merits did they cultivate?"—
from these two phrases, one hears of their causal practices,
through which they were able to possess such great supernormal powers.
These two lines inquire about its fruit;
they concern present virtue.
The preceding section clarifies past causes.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Having practiced which samādhi," etc.:
this is the second question. These two [powers] share a common cause; they do not arise in isolation, for their arising must necessarily depend upon meditative concentration (samādhi).
"How should one practice samādhi? I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this samādhi to me.
From "I pray... onwards is the third question concerning the physical marks of his body; from "The Buddha said... onwards is the Tathāgata’s response.
From the passage beginning with "from the very beginning" down to "because he saw Mañjuśrī, his body came here," this is the answer to the third question.
Regarding the reason why Many Treasures was commanded [to appear], there are generally two meanings.
First, it clarifies that the origin of the birth of Prabhūtaratna as the foremost of those who propagate the sutra is the most supreme.
Second, it clarifies that the two Buddhas share the same mind;
to clarify this principle, each causes light to summon [the other].
First, the oral proclamation clarifies that [the Buddha's] intention is non-existent;
second, from the section beginning with "At that time, Many Treasures" onwards,
it correctly explains how Many Treasures issues the command to Gadgadasvara.
From the passage beginning with "At that time,
Gadgadasvara... onwards, it clearly explains how Gadgadasvara, having received the holy decree,
came to this land to offer gifts and perform worship, and to inquire after [the Buddha's] well-being in accordance with propriety.
"I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
This request to see him is briefly stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter;
its later detailed exposition regarding the same matter is no different from the request made by Mahāpratibhāna to see him.
It remains here for the sake of authenticating and circulating [the teaching].
This clarification, as well as the vision of Mañjuśrī,
refers to witnessing the deeds performed by that Mañjuśrī.
From the passage where Puṣpadatta addressed the Buddha at that time,
down to the point where it is said that this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has deeply planted roots of goodness—
this is because the answer is remote from the question; therefore, he is raised again to request the response.
The one above asked: "What roots of goodness did you plant?
What merits did you clarify to possess such supernormal powers? [The Buddha replied:
"In the past, with various musical instruments from the ten directions and bowls made of the seven precious gems, [I made offerings to] the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna."
This is the gathering of internal conditions, and this is its cause.
This is the fruit of its practice.
Now, this supernormal power arises from retribution.
This refers to his merit.
From the passage "From you, it is seen that although his wondrous voice is here...
onwards, there is an extensive explanation of the merit of his present retribution.
From the point below one hundred thousand Ganges Rivers,
I wish to speak of the Wondrous Sound;
it is not only in this region.
Furthermore, in other directions and through various manifestations of transformation,
there are those who have deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of Gadgadasvara.

This is the statement by Puṣpadatta expressing his understanding; from the words "World-Honored One, in which samādhi does this bodhisattva abide," he again raises the second question to request its answer.
In response to the previous question regarding which samādhi constitutes such conduct,
the answer now given is that it is named "Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
This is the Flower Samādhi of the Dharma-body, wherein the six sense faculties are purified.
Regarding the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara": This person is likewise a Mahāsattva of the Dharmakāya.
Belonging to the lineage of Wondrous Sound (Ghoṣa), he should originally have been in the Western Land;
however, having a karmic affinity with this land, he came here for private transformation.
Because he universally responds through all gateways and delivers sentient beings by means of his voice, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
He is the wondrous sound of the world;
he is so named because he transforms people through the sounds that issue from himself.
This Avalokiteśvara derives his name from "previous sounds.
He observes the preceding sounds and proceeds to deliver beings; it is for this reason that he is so named.

Within this chapter, there are six sections in total: first, from the beginning down to the end of the passage on the name of Avalokiteśvara, which establishes his title; second, from "If, moreover, there should be a person... onwards.
It is thus exceedingly sublime.
This is intended to clarify that among all names for beings in this world, Avalokiteśvara is the most great in benefiting others;
for he excels all in the benefit of uprooting suffering and rescuing those in distress.
The subsequent scripture states: "Sublime and majestic it is thus. The third section, from "If there are sentient beings" onwards, concludes with the benefits of merit.
This describes that Avalokiteśvara is called "Contemplating Sound," is called "Contemplating Mindfulness," and is also called "Contemplating Form."
However, the name of this land as "the Place of Benefit" (Yichu) also surpasses its physical form and mind.
From the passage beginning with "For this reason," below,
he concludes by praising the excellence of its name and exhorting people [to practice].
"Receiving and upholding" refers to the name [of this practice].
From the passage beginning with "If there is anyone...
onwards, it is a comparative evaluation showing that the benefit of the name is superior to that of others.
Therefore, it is said that receiving the names of more than six hundred and twenty million bodhisattvas is not equal to upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara.
This is intended to clarify that the scope of Avalokiteśvara’s transformative influence is superior to that of other bodhisattvas.
This refers to the section beginning from "The sentient beings who maintain the exhaustion of outflows" up until the end of the chapter where the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addresses the Buddha,
concluding with the Vajrapāṇi deity’s explanation of the meaning of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha).
To extensively clarify that his virtue is inexhaustible,
three questions are posed herein:
"How does he roam throughout the Sahā world?"
Question: What forms do you assume through skillful means?
How do you benefit all living beings and preach the Dharma for them?
Question: Through what skillful means do you preach what kind of Dharma?
Regarding the power of skillful means (*upāya*) for transforming sentient beings, what are its specific activities?
This summarizes the two preceding meanings in form.

As for the question of how the activities of skillful means are ultimately carried out: it refers to the manifestation of the Buddha’s body by the Tathāgata for those who should receive benefit by beholding the Buddha’s body.
To clarify that the Sage’s responses take diverse forms according to the six realms, appearing in accordance with the perceptions of sentient beings:
if one employs expedient forms to preach the Dharma,
the teaching will differ according to the faculties and natures of those beings.

The answer states that the second [question] is answered through the "skillful means" (upāya) response, and there is no separate text for it. From the fifth section, beginning with "Having thus accomplished these [qualities], Ajita, Avalokiteśvara," down to the passage on his traveling through the Sahā world.
To clarify that Avalokiteśvara bestows grace upon sentient beings and to exhort people to make offerings to him:
for this reason, because Avalokiteśvara manifests forms and responds with the six supernormal powers to the infinite [beings],
one should receive his teachings in their entirety and offer worship.
Regarding the one who can bestow fearlessness:
among the four kinds of giving, the gift of fearlessness is the most supreme. What are these four?
First is the gift of material wealth; second is the gift of the Hīnayāna;
third is the gift of the Mahāyāna;
and fourth is the gift of fearlessness.
Because he is the most supreme among all and because he is worthy of offerings, he is called by five names; thus he is named "Bestower of Fearlessness.

Precious jewels are material wealth.
Why, then, is it said that those who receive this Dharma-gift do so with the intention of inexhaustibility?

There are two reasons why Avalokiteśvara initially did not accept [the offerings]:

As for the reason why [the recipient] subsequently accepts it:
knowing that by accepting it at this assembly and dedicating it back [to the donor], one can thereby understand the Dharma-body of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), they accept it.
For this reason, it is divided into two types of giving.
The mention of "two Buddhas" is intended to clarify that the Buddha represents the ultimate fruit.
It correctly demonstrates that all wholesome virtues converge toward this wondrous fruit, and that in principle there are no divergent paths.
This signifies the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Second, it is intended to clarify that giving one portion to the Buddha and one portion to sentient beings is meant to manifest that both arising and ceasing are expedient means (*upāya*).

Based on this, the *dharmakāya* is the true reality; the circulation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is precisely found in this passage. Sixth, from "At that time, the Earth-holding [Bodhisattva]" onwards.
Regarding the phrase "all that benefits beings at the time of completion issues forth from the Peerless One":

That the Buddhas possess realization is what is termed "Equal" (sama).
Regarding the "Dhāraṇī Chapter": from this point onward, the purpose of the text is to clarify the correct method for future generations, as many obstacles and hindrances will abound therein.
If one does not apply protective transformation, it will be difficult to cause the teaching to flow forth; therefore, because it is necessary to use dhāraṇīs for protection, this chapter exists.
Second, as for the Great Being who has accumulated merit over vast eons, his practice is profound and lofty;

having eliminated all internal and external defilements, what need is there to wait for protection when proclaiming the teachings in this degenerate age? As for those who speak of "protection," it is as follows:
If the disciples listening to the Dharma do not understand or lack firm faith,

By protecting the disciples so that the path of transformation is applied appropriately, one thereby protects the Dharma Master as well.
Within this chapter, there are four sections in total:

The merit [of this] is exceedingly great, O Tathāgata.
It is precisely for the sake of those who uphold this sutra that the merit is immeasurable.
Making offerings to the various Buddhas and practicing the wholesome roots of scattering [flowers and incense] constitute their meritorious karma.

How much more so when one upholds the sutras and maintains the purity of the three marks while dwelling in the midst of the Dharma; at such times, understanding this is the activity of wisdom, which is likewise lofty and supreme.
This is precisely because it transcends inferior reliance on merit; therefore, it is said that even a single four-line verse [is of great value].
To fully demonstrate that the lower support (āśraya) possesses few instances where its attainment accords with principle, whereas the upper support’s virtues are always far more numerous—
how much more so for both supports together—
is the reason these two supports are presented as immeasurable.

The section on virtue begins with the text that provides a comparison from below; third, it extends from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha" down to "one should protect such Dharma-preachers."
This clearly explains the protective empowerment of mantras spoken by various individuals.

The fifth section concerns the Rakṣasīs who protect both by means of their bodies and mantras.
From the passage where the Buddha has finished instructing the various Rakṣasīs onwards,

If you merely protect the disciples who rely upon the four requisites, the names of the sutras alone will be immeasurable; how much more so for those who fully receive and uphold the protective mantras!
These mantras shall protect the Dharma masters, enabling them to circulate [the teachings] now without interruption, such that their transformative merit and blessings shall likewise flourish.
"Immeasurable. Following the fourth chapter, "The Exposition of this Dhāraṇī," the subsequent sections clarify the benefits for that time.

From the chapter "The King of Sublime Adornment" onwards, it is intended to instruct sentient beings that in the future they should rely upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), just as the King of Sublime Adornment did.
Second, regarding relying on persons as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one should be like the ladies Pure Treasury, Pure Eye, and Pure Virtue.
Within this chapter, there are five sections in total; the first begins from the start and concludes with the section titled "The Eon Named Joyful Vision."
The section "The Radiant and Wondrous Adornment Relies on the Station of a Spiritual Friend" (second part, from "From the Buddha-dharma... onwards) concludes with "delighting in the Buddha-dharma.
This correctly clarifies that the three sages jointly transform the heterodox king, causing him to give rise to right views; it is intended to clarify the benefits of this transformation.
First, let us hear the names of the two individuals.
From the passage beginning with "These two sons possessed great supernatural power," it is extensively praised that these two sons,
possessing such lofty virtues, were surely capable of transforming the heterodox and giving rise to correct faith.
The text is abbreviated and does not praise the virtue of that person.
From that time onward, that Buddha, wishing to guide them by preaching the Lotus Sutra, brought forth those individuals and caused them to emerge with the medicine of the Dharma.
The reason I, your elder son, requested that you come together with me to the Buddha’s dwelling was because I wished to share with the heterodox king the karmic conditions for his transformation.
You ought to go and fulfill your duty as my father, and thus we shall depart together.
This clarifies the conditions for transformation and the persons to be transformed,

Having witnessed these divine transformations, he turned his back on the heterodox and returned to the Right Path; thus were his spiritual faculties awakened. Third, from "Thereupon, King Subhavyūha... down to "...the merits of that land were thus perfected."

"Even though they have understood and joyfully praised it"— the fifth section, from "The Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment" onwards through the end of the chapter,

From the "Chapter on Samantabhadra": This person is a Great Being (Mahāsattva) of the Dharma-body.

Within the second section, the exhortation regarding future lives, there are six textual passages. The first, beginning from "First" and ending with "one will surely obtain this sutra," intends to clarify the two bases for its circulation in the future.

This clarifies that the Tathāgata recounts the exhortations of Samantabhadra regarding the two bases [of reliance].

Wishing to cause the Tathāgata to emerge from the lower levels of reliance,

this is precisely the characteristic of relying below.
"One who accomplishes four dharmas shall obtain this sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa;
such a person shall circulate the sutra.
What are these four practices? First, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas."
Having already cultivated the lineage of practice,
they are likewise protected and remembered; yet, because they have not yet attained the profound principle,
their understanding differs from that of a Buddha and they still remain subject to regression.
They are not given the name "protected.
From the stage of the nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) upward, they attain a profound understanding that is identical to that of a Tathāgata;
being necessarily firm and non-retrogressive, their merit is given the name "protected. Second, regarding the planting of the roots of all virtues:
Initially, based on the five constant practices of the Great Being, he extensively accumulated the myriad deeds;

First, attaining the stage of the nature of reality (gotrabhūmi) such that one never regresses is called "right determination" (samyaktva-niyāma). Fourth, regarding the arousal of the mind to rescue sentient beings:

"He will certainly be able to circulate this sutra.

As for "riding the six-tusked white elephant," it means:

To clarify that for a Mahāsattva there are only the ten thousand practices for transforming sentient beings, and that among these, nothing is more essential than the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), he therefore rides upon the six tusks.

These metaphors are employed by taking up the quality of strength and the causal factors to illustrate this matter.

This refers to the inferior disciple of this chapter,
who possesses only the wisdom derived from hearing.
From the point where it says, "If one sits and contemplates after meeting such a person," and so forth.

This ability to contemplate constitutes a superior wisdom of reflection;
having already surpassed the medium level of clear knowledge previously mentioned,
he further appears before one riding a white elephant.
This is because he manifests himself accordingly.
If there are those who have forgotten the Lotus Sutra,

Because he infers the arising of conceptual understanding from past conditions and then regresses, [the Buddha] teaches according to the occasion to cause him to subdue his fundamental misconceptions;
thus, I describe this as teaching to bring about thorough mastery.
The Great Being adapts to capacities and manifests speech for the benefit of others, moistening them extensively; his diligent application of the mind is such that it never ceases.
It is said that upon attaining [this], they experience great joy and become even more diligent.

"From the latter five hundred years in this world of evil merit onwards,

The karmic fruit of propagating this sutra in the future will be great.

This begins from the words "From the praise of Śākyamuni... and below.

Now, the Tathāgata again reiterates the words from the "Chapter on the Encouragement of Samantabhadra" regarding the disciples of the three grades:

"Furthermore, I myself shall constantly protect those who uphold the name of Samantabhadra;

It is clear that the merit of a disciple who upholds this sutra is already vast;
how much more so for the two bases (*āśraya*), which have not yet been described. Following this, there is a separate passage concerning disciples:

"If there are those who receive and uphold [it]," without explicitly titling it as the "Universal Worthy’s Exhortation to the Two Bases. You previously stated that these two bases shall circulate this sutra in the future.
